REGULATIONS GOVERNING HELICOPTER OPERATIONS
6. The regulatory control of helicopter operations are covered under the Aircraft Act 1937,
Aircraft Rules 1937 and the Civil Aviation Requirements (CARs) issued from time to time under
these Rules. However, due to peculiarity of the helicopters, mainly in terms of design, basic
operating principles and operating procedures, certain CARs, Aeronautical Circulars (AICs) and
Advisory Circulars specifically meant for helicopter operations, have also been issued.
7. The training requirements for helicopter pilots have been elaborated in CAR Section 7. The
operating regulations for helicopter operations are based on ICAO Annex 6 Part III and have been
adopted in the form of CAR Section 2 Series O Part IV and V for commercial and private
helicopter operations respectively. The regulations are updated from time to time in accordance with
the amendments introduced by ICAO in Annex 6 Part III, after consultation with the helicopter
industry.
8. To a specific query on the mechanism/rules/regulations/provisions available with DGCA to
ensure that the helicopter pilots follow the laid down rules and regulations, the Committee was
informed that helicopter pilots are subjected to annual proficiency check by the DGCA approved
Examiner for their renewal of licenses. Besides, pilots are subjected to surveillance from time to
time to ensure that they follow regulations.
9. To a further query on the guidelines for operating helicopters in poor visibility conditions
and the action taken by DGCA for violation of such guidelines during the recent years, the
Committee was informed that the guidelines are given in AIP India, ENR 1.1.3, Para 6; CAR
Section 4, Series E Part I,  Para 3.9 and CAR Section 8, Series O Part 1, Para 3. The Committee
was further informed by the Ministry of Civil Aviation that in poor visibility helicopters are
permitted to operate special VFR flights subject to the following conditions:
(a) When traffic conditions permit, special VFR flights can be authorized subject to the
approval from the unit providing approach control service.
(b) When the ground visibility is not less than 1500 meters, ATC can authorize special
VFR flights provided the helicopter is certified for IFR operations.
(c) Helicopters can be authorized under special VFR for operations in Performance Class
I and Class II when ground visibility is not less than 1000 meters. For such
authorizations, pilot is responsible for meeting the criteria for operations in
performance class I and class II and is required to reflect the same in the flight plan
and report on RT to A TC.

3
(d) For operating helicopter in visibility up to 1000 meters, the helicopter is required to
be maneuvered at a speed that will give adequate opportunity to observe other traffic
or any obstacle in time to avoid collusion.
10. The Ministry further stated that in the recent past, there has been one case of such violation
by one of the Pawan Hans Helicopter-VT-PHR engaged in VIP flight. The helicopter made landing
after sunset. DGCA carried out the investigation and de-rostered the pilot during the course of
investigation. The pilot was later counseled.
DGCA INITIATIVES
11. The Committee was further informed that in order to take effective measures for improving
the safety record of helicopter operations in the country, a helicopter cell in DGCA has been
formed. The cell is headed by a Joint Director General and has experts from airworthiness,
aerodrome standards, air safety and flight operations directorates of DGCA as well as
representatives from the industry, namely PHHL and Rotary Wing Society of India (RWSI). The
objectives and responsibilities of the helicopter cell are as follows:
(i) Review and updating of standards of airworthiness and operations of helicopters in
consultation with helicopter industry;
(ii) Stipulate requirements for operations from improvised helipads, temporary helipads
for seasonal operations, heliports, roof-top operations and other aerial work
operations. This will include the requirements for preparation of Standard Operating
Procedures (SOPs), Minimum Equipment List (MEL), Maintenance Programme and
other technical documents and their approval;
(iii) Plan and conduct audits of helicopter operators including off-shore operations on
annual basis and follow-up on the observations of audits;
(iv) Revision of relevant sections of Schedule II of the Aircraft Rules, dealing with PPL,
CPL and ATPL (helicopters) in line with international standards as per ICAO Annex/
EASA regulations;
(v) Review of FDTL regulations for helicopter pilots;
(vi) Approval of Operations Manual of NSOP applicants (helicopters) and association with
preparedness meetings for the grant of NSOP for helicopter operators. This may
include demonstration flights and demonstration of operational procedures (load and
trim, flight dispatch, evacuation, passenger facilities, FDTL monitoring, flight data
evaluation, external load applications etc.);
(vii) Inspection of helipads for seasonal operations and approval for SOPs for such
operations;
(viii) Coordination with AAI for approval of separate procedures for helicopter operations;
(ix) Matters related to creation of heliports including identification of sites and related
follow-up;
(x) Conducting annual meetings with helicopter operators to review the areas of concern
expressed by them from time-to-time, and the necessary follow-up;
(xi) Compiling and analyzing statistics of helicopter pilots, AMEs, hours of operation in
different categories, surveillance observations, audit findings, etc.

4
12. The Emergency Locater Transmitter (ELT) is a tracking transmitter which aids in the
detection and location of aircraft in distress. The Committee asked about the availability and
operation of ELT in aircrafts and choppers operating in the country. The Committee was informed
that a one-time check of all aircraft operating in the country was carried out by DGCA. During
the check, it was found that out of 1029 operating aircrafts, 909 aircrafts are fitted with ELTs
capable of operating with dual frequency (121.5 and 406 MHz). The remaining 120 aircrafts are
fitted with ELTs capable of operating only on 121.5 MHz. DGCA has issued guidelines to install
ELTs conforming to 406 MHz frequency when operating in Designated land Areas. Earlier, the ELTs
conforming to 406 MHz were not installed due to the reason that Designated land Areas were not
notified by the Airports Authority of India. However, now all operators have been advised to install
ELTs capable of transmitting signals on both 121.5 MHz and 406 MHz frequency by 31/03/2010
irrespective of such notification. During the intervening period, operators have been advised to
avoid operations in hilly terrain and inaccessible areas in case their aircraft is fitted with ELT
conforming to only 121.5 MHz frequency.
SPREADING SAFETY AWARENESS
13. In order to promote safety awareness amongst the personnel involved in helicopter
operations, the DGCA has organized several seminars and a few accident data analysis workshops
at national and international level. An international seminar was held in July 2007 in association with
DGAC France and another seminar was held in association with International Helicopter Safety
Team (IHST) and RWSI. R WSI is also approved to carry out short capsule courses on Special
VFR operations for helicopter pilots.
14. Seminars and the courses for helicopter pilots and engineers have resulted in awareness of
safety issues in respects of helicopter operations. Special meetings are organized and safety
circulars issued prior to Centre/State elections due to increasing use of helicopters by VIPs during
elections. These activities have manifested in improvement in helicopter safety record.
15. When the Committee pointed out the implementation of recommendations of the committees
set up to look into various accidents involving helicopters, it was informed that those
recommendations are being duly addressed. The Committee was further informed that State
Governments’ infrastructure are the main obstacle for a proper planning of helicopter operations.
The State Governments have been advised to build proper infrastructure with meteorological
briefing arrangements, flight planning arrangements and information about obstacles on the way.
The Committee was further informed that the State Governments have been advised to follow the
Civil Aviation Requirements on the helicopter operations issued by the Central Government from
time-to-time.
DEDICATED HELIPORTS AND OPERATING CORRIDORS
16. When the Committee drew the attention of the Ministry towards the increasing number of
helicopter operators in the country and the lack of adequate infrastructure for the industry, the
Ministry of Civil Aviation replied that it had already appointed a committee to identify sites where
heliports could be  built for facilitating the operations without interfering with the normal air traffic
at busy airports. As a result, a dedicated area for heliport has been earmarked at Delhi airport
where a heliport could be built for operations without interfering in the normal traffic. Presently,
AAI are developing special procedures for helicopter operations from the proposed heliports.
Similarly, at Mumbai special procedures have been devised for helicopter operations from Juhu
airport for which trials are being conducted.
17. PHHL has also been allotted substantial area at Sector 37, Rohini, Delhi for establishment
of an MRO and operations facilities. Another heliport is slated to be established in Central Delhi
for convenience of commuters.

TRAINING FACILITIES FOR PILOTS
18. The Committee was informed that due to increasing number of helicopters in the country,
there is an urgent need for dedicated helicopter training organization in India. Presently, HAL has
a training academy for helicopter pilots which, however, is inadequate to meet the requirements of
the helicopter industry. To fill up this gap, PHHL has been offered adequate land at the DGCA
managed gliding centre at Pune to establish training academy for pilots. It is also proposed that
National Aviation Training Academy at Gondia will have a helicopter training unit. Once the two
training academies are operational, the gap of demand and supply for civil helicopter pilots is
expected to be eliminated.
19. The Committee was further informed that for 285 helicopters operating in the country,
around 600 pilots are available at an estimate of two-and-a-half sets of pilots for each helicopter.
The Ministry admitted the shortage of pilots for helicopter industry at present.
20. As far as the training facilities available in the country for helicopter pilots, the Committee
was informed that simulator training is considered essential for initial and periodic training of
helicopter pilots as it helps in training pilots to simulate and practice real-time emergency situations.
Presently, one fixed simulator has been established in private sector in Delhi. A full motion simulator
is being established by a HAL-CAE JV company at Bangalore and is expected to be operational by
mid 2010. These state-of-the--art simulator facilities will be capable of adapting docking stations
and Cockpit environment of Bell, Eurocopter and Dhruv helicopters. These initiatives will go a long
way in helping the pilots to cope up with emergency situations.
21. DGCA has also approved a number “of training institutes for imparting ab initio training on
helicopter maintenance. Apart from some of the existing AME training Institutes, PHHL Training
Institute has recently been approved to impart such training. It is apparent that a foundation has
been made for systematic flying and maintenance training which will form the basis for
enhancement of safe helicopter operations in India.
22. During the deliberations of the Committee, it was informed that 80-90 per cent of the civil
fleet comprise of ex-military pilots who have thousands of hours of experience in all kinds of
adverse weather conditions and challenging conditions. The training standards of Indian helicopter
fleet are very high as compared to other countries.
23. The Committee was further informed that the Ministry of Civil Aviation has devised a
procedure to convert some fixed wing pilots into helicopter pilots, since helicopter training is an
expensive proposition. The DGCA has chalked out a regulation that after giving 80 hours training
on helicopter operations, the fixed wing pilots will be given an option to convert themselves as
helicopter pilots. It was further informed that Pawan Hans Helicopters Limited entered into an
agreement with the Air Force and Navy to induct the retired pilots in their wings. Pawan Hans
Helicopters Limited will start the induction of retired pilots on the basis of their profile.
SAFETY AUDITS AND SURVEILLANCE BY DGCA
24. To a query on the annual check audit of helicopter operators, the Ministry informed that
a periodic audit of all helicopter operators is conducted under the planned annual audit and
surveillance programme formulated by DGCA. In addition, special audits have also been planned to
conduct the following audits in the near future:
• Audit of all State Government /Public Sector Undertaking aviation organizations.
• Audit of off-shore helicopter operations and safety aspects at off-shore rigs.

6
25. These audits bring out non-compliance and deficiencies vis-a-vis operating regulations, on
which DGCA takes strict enforcement action in accordance with the laid down procedures. With
the recent augmentation plan of workforce in DGCA, it will now be possible to undertake the
surveillance and audit work in a more vigorous manner. Helicopter division in Flight Standards
Directorate (FSD), DGCA now has four dedicated Flight Operations Inspectors and FSD will now
be in a position to undertake the helicopter related responsibilities in an effective manner.
HELICOPTER ACCIDENT
26. Helicopter operations occasionally come to adverse notice as and when there are some
accidents/incidents involving helicopters. Recent occurrences of the forcible landing/take-off and
helicopters accidents in bad light during the VIP movements, raised the question of existence of
a regulator for helicopter operations in the country. These accidents questioned the effectiveness
of the existing safety and security norms regulating helicopter operation in the country.
27. The Committee was informed that there were seven accidents involving the India Civil
registered helicopters during the period 2007 to 2009. All the accidents were investigated by the
DGCA and the probable causes were identified. The causes recorded were:-
(i) Uncontrollable movement of helicopter during hover exercise and delayed corrective
action by instructor resulted in crash landing of helicopter;
(ii) During landing main rotor blades hit ground crew;
(iii) Non-adherence of Standard Operating Procedures wherein the flight crew failed to
maintain adequate terrain clearance. Bad weather and improper crew detailing who
were not qualified for such operations was the contributory factor;
(iv) During landing pilot experienced loss of tail rotor effectiveness and entered into right
yaw due to changing wind conditions which resulted in loss of control and crash
landing of helicopter. Wrong location of the windsock at the helipad was contributory
factor to the accident.
(v) Helicopter descended below the minimum safe altitude due to bad weather and
collided with the hill en route. Contributory factors are crew did not obtain the
meteorological briefing the departure and selection of improper route by the crew.
(vi) During landing, the helicopter encountered operational problems and landed around
500 meters before the helipad.
(vii) Accident occurred due to loss of control resulting in uncontrolled descent in the
terrain at a very high rate of descent due to entry into severe downdraught.
Contributory factors (i) crew noticed a snag and was engrossed for more than vital
six minutes before the impact in searching for relevant information in the emergency
check list and Flight manual. (ii) The crew was flying in Instrument Meteorological
Conditions (IMC) whereas the flight was cleared for VFR flying and (iii) They had
no intention either to divert or return back to base.

GENERAL OBSERV ATIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS
29. The Committee observes that even after a period of almost six decades since its
inception, the helicopter operations in India is still in a rudimentary stage as compared to
that in the western countries in terms of existence of a separate regulatory mechanism,
rules and regulations as well as necessary infrastructure specific to helicopters. The
Committee found that currently, the helicopter operations i.e. rotary wing aircrafts are
being governed by the set of rules, regulations and mechanism under the DGCA which are
meant for the fixed wing aircraft. In view of significant differences between the two, the
Committee feels that there is an urgent need to put mechanism, rules, regulations and the
required infrastructure specific to the helicopter sector in place, without further delay.
30. The Committee also found that currently, helicopters are being used mainly for VIP
operations and transporting people to offshore oil operations. The Committee feels that the
Government has not taken enough steps for expansion of helicopter sector in India. The
Committee is of the opinion that helicopter operations have to be expanded to such other
areas as tourism, medical emergencies, disaster management, maintenance of law and
order, etc.
31. In this connection, the Committee would like to make special mention about the use
of helicopters in medical emergency, a strong case for which was made out by the
representatives of the Rotary Wing Society of India before the Committee. The Committee
is also convinced that this country holds a huge potential for using helicopters in this area.
Many lives can be saved by bringing the accident victims from remote and inaccessible areas
for providing immediate medical help during golden hour. The Committee would like that

8
a Feasibility Study may be got conducted by involving all the stakeholders, government as
well as private, to promote the use of helicopters in those areas.
32. The Committee also feels that promotion of tourism to remote and inaccessible areas
can be done by making helicopters services available for the tourists to such places. The
Committee recommends that the Government should take steps to make heli-tourism more
attractive and affordable by reducing cost of operation through fiscal incentives, lowering
taxes on ATF, waiving off RNFC, rationalizing landing and parking charges after
consultation with the State Governments.
33. Presently, we are having 250 odd helicopters in operation, which are likely to be
increased significantly in the coming areas. In view of the great potential for helicopter
travel in the country, urgent need for dedicated helicopter training organizations can hardly
be over-emphasized. The Committee is not aware about the future requirement of the
trained manpower for the helicopter sector. One gliding centre at Pune and one training
academy at Gondia have been proposed. Currently, we have one fixed simulator in private
sector in Delhi and one full motion simulator is being established by HAL at Bangalore. The
existing training facilities, thus, are inadequate to meet the future requirements of the
industry. The Committee does not know about the status of those centres that were being
set up. It would like to have a status report in respect of the proposed centres.
34. The Committee recommends that the Government should address the issue of
shortage of helicopter pilots on priority since the industry is gaining momentum rapidly The
Committee feels that the Government should appoint a Committee of experts to review the
present system of examination and procedures for award of licenses to pilots. It may
consider creating of national pool of independent examiners, standardize the syllabi,
increase the frequency of examinations and rationalize the charges for skill tests.
35. The Committee further notes that for monitoring proficiency of pilots operating over
250 helicopters, DGCA is having four helicopter Inspectors on secondment basis from the
industry. The Committee feels that efforts should be made to have more Inspectors who are
type qualified and in current flying. In the longer term, the Committee feels that there is
a need to have adequate number of Flight Inspectors with long experience to handle
proficiency monitoring of pilots. While doing so, our future requirements should be kept in
mind.
36. The Committee notes that a number of agencies such as PSUs, corporate houses and
the State Governments are operating helicopters in India. The Committee, therefore, feels
that their involvement will play a major role in providing requisite infrastructure for
helicopter operations in the country. The Committee, therefore, recommends that wider
consultations needs to be done with all the stakeholders while creating a regulatory
mechanism for this purpose.
37. The Committee notes with concern the instances of forceful landing/take off of
helicopters in low visibility, bad weather and even during nights, which are serious breaches
of aviation security norms. It has been brought to the notice of the Committee that at
times technical clearances are given to the helicopters with minor defects to take off. The
technical personnel including pilots are put under pressure not to oppose these deficiencies
due to commercial or other reasons. It happens mainly in the case of chartered helicopters
and those under the State Governments flying VIPs. Such violations of rules have led to
fatal accidents losing several precious lives. Lack of proper maintenance and non-
observance of operating manuals, mechanical failures and lack of required instruments have
been found as the causes of these accidents. It points out towards the ineffectiveness of

9
safety audit and mandatory inspections of the helicopters and other facilities for testing
their airworthiness. The Committee recommends that technical personnel/pilots be provided
adequate legal/administrative protection to decline to fly in the absence of mandatory
technical, weather and other clearances. Some kind of penal provision may be considered
against those putting such pressure on the pilots to fly without proper clearances.
Conversely, the strictest actions be taken against those pilots/technicians who violate these
requirements even under some kind of duress. Their licences may be immediately cancelled
if prime facie they appear to have done so.
38. In order to ensure independent and impartial enquiry into accidents, the Committee
would like to reiterate its earlier recommendation made in its 168th Report which is
reproduced below:
“The Committee is of the view that creation of an independent authority for accident
investigation on an urgent basis will instill confidence in the minds of travelling public.”
39. The Committee recommends that the entire gamut of helicopter operations in India
may be reviewed and adequate/appropriate steps may be taken to ensure safer helicopter
travel. The Committee recommends that guidelines/regulations for take off/landing of
helicopters during low visibility should not only be strengthened but enforced strictly.
40. The Committee notes that Helicopter Cell has been set up in the DGCA. It, however,
is surprised to find that the Helicopter Cell within the DGCA does not have representation
of AAI that provides ATC services. Though there is a provision of coordination with AAI,
the Committee is of the view that for better coordination between AAI and DGCA in this
matter, it would only be appropriate, if AAI is permanently represented in the Helicopter
Cell of the DGCA. The Committee would also like to be informed of the details of the
major observations/decisions made by the Helicopter Cell and the Action Taken for
implementation thereof.
41. For expanding the helicopter operations to the newer areas as has been suggested by
the Committee elsewhere, India will have to have a number of heliports, vertiports and
heli-routes in the country. The Committee also emphasizes the need for developing a
network of helipads and heliports in and around metros as well as in the hilly and remote
parts of the country. The Committee is of the opinion that a dedicated heliport wing may
be established in the Airports Authority of India to oversee the development of heliports
and vertiports and heli-routes in the country.
42. The Committee feels that a concerted coordination mechanism involving Union and
State Governments, meteorological department and other agencies should be evolved to
make helicopter operations safer one. The existing Air Traffic Rules may be reviewed to
eliminate delays in helicopter departures/arrivals from major airports. Flight routing may be
made as direct as possible independent of fixed wing traffic to ease the congestion at the
airports.
43. Since the LTC travellers now constitute a significant number, the Committee is
surprised to find that under CCS (LTC) Rules, they are not allowed to travel by Helicopters.
The Committee is of the view that LTC travellers should also be allowed to travel by
helicopters and the matter may be taken up with the Ministry of Personnel, Public
Grievances and Pensions for amendment of the LTC rules accordingly.
44. The Committee is surprised to note that around 120 aircrafts which might include
helicopters were not capable of operating in hilly terrains and the operators of such
aircrafts have been advised not to operate in such areas till the necessary instruments

10
(ELTs conforming to 406 MHz) were fitted. Deadline given for this was 31-3-2010. In such
a situation, the Committee feels that the possibility of such aircrafts operating in hilly
areas cannot be ruled out, particularly in view of the lax and inadequate monitoring in the
sector. The Committee only hopes that these instruments would have been placed by the
given date, and if not, all such aircrafts should be grounded and not allowed to fly until they
have compiled with this.
45. The Committee has been informed by the Ministry that the main obstacle for the
proper planning of the helicopter operations has been the lack of proper infrastructure with
the State Governments and they have been advised to build proper infrastructure with
meteorological briefing and to follow the civil aviation requirements issued from the Union
Ministry of Civil Aviation from time to time. The Committee is constrained to note that the
Ministry of Civil Aviation has failed to ensure the cooperation and compliance from the
State Governments for helicopter operations. It, therefore, recommends that the Ministry
may take up these issues with the concerned State Governments proactively to get the
needful done.

INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport,
Tourism and Culture, having been authorised by the Committee to present on its behalf, do hereby
present this One Hundred and Seventieth Report on “Modernization of Major Ports”.
2. Despite a long coastline and long history of maritime activities in the country from centuries
back, the traffic handled by a single international port is more than the traffic handled by all the
Indian Ports put together. As such to take account of what ails the Indian Shipping Sector, the
Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture decided
to take up the examination of the functioning of major ports . The Committee reviewed the
upgradation of Indian Ports and the projects under National Maritime Development Programme
which cover the entire gamut of activities proposed for the port modernization target.
3. On 9
th February, 2010, the Committee heard the Secretary, Ministry of Shipping to get an
overview of the subject. The Committee conducted study visits in two phases and visited Kolkata,
Chennai and Kochi in the first phase and covered Haldia - Kolkata, Chennai, Ennore, Tuticorin and
Cochin Ports. During the second phase Paradip, Mumbai, Jawaharlal Nehru, New Mangalore,
Mormugao, Kandla and Visakhapatnam Ports were covered. The Committee heard the views of all
the 12 Port Managements. The Committee also interacted with the stake holders and port
employees unions of various ports during the visits. Thereafter the Committee sought clarifications
from the Ministry of Shipping and heard the views of the Secretary of Ministries of Shipping, Road
Transport and Highways, and the Ministry of Railways on the 20
th December, 2010 on various
aspects of modernization of ports.
4. The. Committee wishes to express its thanks to the Secretary and other officers of the
Ministry of Shipping, Ministry of Road Transport and Highways, Ministry of Railways, Officials
and Employees of the Major Ports for providing necessary inputs and clarifications during
deliberations on the subject.  The Committee also acknowledges the contribution of the unions/
Associations who submitted their valuable suggestions on the subject.
5. The Committee considered and adopted the Report at its meeting held on the 27
th May, 2011.
SITARAM YECHURY
NEW D ELHI; Chairman,
May 27, 2011 Department-related Parliamentary Standing
Jyaishtha 6, 1933  (Saka) Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture.

1
REPORT
Introduction
There are 12 Major Ports (6 in the east coast and 6 on the west coast) and 187 Minor
Ports in India. The Major Ports are under the control of the Central Government and the minor
ports are under the control of State Governments. Ports provide an interface between the ocean
transport and land-based transport. About 95% by volume and 7% by value of the country’s
external merchandise trade is carried out through maritime transport. The country’s long coastline
of around 7517 km. spread on the western and eastern shelves of the mainland and also along the
islands is a natural resource capable of being harnessed for the country’s trade and tourism
development. The Indian shipping industry not only transports national and international cargoes but
also provides various other facilities such as shipbuilding, ship repairing, lighthouse facilities, freight
forwarding, etc.
2. The main functions of the Major Parts are cargo handling: loading the cargo vessels for
export and unloading the cargo brought by import. Major Ports, however, have to undertake several
ancillary functions; dredging, maintenance of navigational channels, pilotage, berthing, buoying,
bunkering, dry docking including chipping and painting, maintenance of lighthouses and so on. The
multifarious activities make the Port a huge and complex organization. The Indian Major Ports
maintain hospitals, schools/colleges, and guest houses and as such, the number of work force
appears to be on high side when compared with the International Ports.
3. In India, the Major Ports are placed under the Union List of the Constitution, and are
administered under the Indian Ports Act, 1908 and the Major Port Trust Act, 1963 by the
Government of India. Under the Major Port Trust Act, each Port is governed by a Board of
Trustees constituted by the Government of India giving dominance to public enterprises and
government departments. The powers of the trustees are limited and they are bound by directions
on policy matters and orders from the Government of India.
4. Minor Ports are placed in the Concurrent list of the Constitution and are administered under
the Indian Ports Act, 1908. The Act defines the jurisdiction of Central and State Governments over
the Ports. It lays down rules for safety of shipping and conservation of Ports. It regulates matters
pertaining to the administration of Port dues, pilotage fees and other charges.
5. At the State level, the department in-charge of ports or the State Maritime Board is
responsible for formulation of water front development policies and plans, regulating and overseeing
the management of state ports, attracting private investment in the development of state ports,
enforcing environmental protection standards etc.
6. Despite such a long coastline and long history of maritime activities in the country from
centuries back, it is a fact that none of our Major Ports is able to develop into a hub such as
Singapore in the East, Dubai & Middle East on the West and Colombo in the South. The traffic
handled by single international Port like Shanghai Port is more than the traffic handled by all the
Indian Ports put together.
7. The Annual Report of the Ministry of Shipping for the year 2010-11 shows the details of
the port sector achievements in terms of traffic, capacity and performance.

11. After the introduction of new economic reforms in the year 1991, there was drastic change
in the policy of the Government with regard to the functioning of the Major Ports. The
Government felt that in the fiercely competitive world and the emerging challenges a structural
change would be required for improvement of functioning of the Ports.
12. Government appointed a Committee headed by S. Sundar on Port Restructuring in India.
This Report throws light on the main factors that have led to inefficiencies in the Indian ports.
The Report states:
“Most Major Ports were originally designed to handle specific categories of cargo which
have declined in time while other types of cargoes gained importance. The ports have not
been able to adjust to the categories of cargo which grew the most. There are thus several
berths for traditional cargo which are under-utilised, and only a few for new cargo, which
are over-utilised. Equipment utilisation is very poor both because equipment is obsolete and
poorly maintained. Over staffing remains rampant and productivity indicators in respect of
cargo and equipment handling continue to be poor. Documentary procedures relating to
cargo handling such as customs clearance requirements are unduly Complicated and time
consuming. Electronic document processing is still to be introduced in all the ports. Port
access facilities and arrangements for moving inbound and outbound cargo are inadequate
and unsatisfactory. Absence of inter-port and intra-port competition which have been
conducive to substantial productivity increases in other countries is absent in India due to
poor inland connectivity and a policy regime that protected domestic ports against
competitive pressures”.
13. As such, to take account of what ails the Indian Ports, the Department-related Parliamentary
Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture decided to examine the functioning of
Major Ports. On the 9
th February, 2009, the Committee heard the Secretary, Ministry of Shipping
to get an overview of the efforts being made for the development and modernization of Shipping
and Port Sector in the country.
14. The Committee made study visits to some of the Major Ports in two phases: it visited
Kolkata, Chennai, Ennore and Cochin Ports in the first phase; and Paradip, Mumbai, Jawaharlal
Nehru and Visakhapatnam Ports in the second phase. The Committee heard the views of all the
12 Port Managements. The Committee also interacted with the Port users, stake holders and Port
employee’s unions of various ports during the visits. Thereafter the Committee sought clarifications
from the Ministry of Shipping and heard the views of the Secretaries, Ministries of Shipping, Road
Transport and Highways, and Railways on the 20
th December, 2010 on various aspects of
modernization of ports.
15. In the meetings held by the Committee with the management of various ports, the officials
gave the details of the extent of mechanization and equipment available in the Ports. They also
submitted the details of ongoing and future plans for capacity additions. The Port-wise detail of
infrastructural facilities and future programmes are given in the succeeding paragraphs.
Mumbai Port
16. Mumbai Port is a fully integrated multipurpose port handling all types of cargo like break
bulk, dry bulk, liquid bulk cargo and containers. The port has extensive wet and dry dock facilities
to meet the normal needs of ship wing of the port. The Port provides services/facilities from
pilotage to berthing, storage to delivery of cargo and ancillary services of running CFS, Railway

Cochin Port
61. The modern Port of Cochin was developed during the period 1920-1940. By 1930-31, the
Port was formally opened for vessels up to 30 feet draught. Cochin was given the status of Major
Port in 1936. The Administration of the Port got vested in a Board of Trustees on 29
th February,
1964 under the Major Port Trusts Act, 1963. Port of Cochin is located at Kochi in Kerala on the
south west India. The Cochin Port is a natural and all weather port.
62. The Committee was informed that its strategic location on the south-west coast of India
is having a commanding position being at the cross roads of the east-west ocean trade. The Port
is a natural gateway to the vast industrial and agricultural produce markets of the south-west India.
The hinterland of the port includes the whole of Kerala and parts of Tamil Nadu and Karnataka.
A study carried out on the traffic flow in the  hinterland of the Port indicates that about 97% of
the total volume of traffic is accounted for by Kerala. The hinterland of Cochin Port has further
spread over to different areas with the  growth or containerization in the country and establishment
of Inland Container Depots at different load centers in India. The Cochin Port with its proximity
to the international sea route between Europe and the far East and Australia can attract a large
number of container lines offering immense sailing opportunities.
63. The Cochin Port has deep draft alongside berths with modern cargo handling equipments
and modern ship to snore cranes provided for container handling. The approach channel up to the
Cochin Gut, is about 1000  meters long with a designed width of 200 meters and maintained
dredged depth of 13.8 meters. From the Gut, the channel divides into Mattancherry channel and
Ernakulam channel, leading to west and east of Willingdon Island respectively and berthing facilities
for ships have been provided in the form of wharves, berths, jetties and stream moorings alongside
these channels.
64. Cochin Port is India’s first e-port having fast documentation and efficient administration of
services bracked by a fully computerized network and single window facility for faster
documentation with modern communication facilities. The Port is having adequate warehousing
capacity and is linked to the Inland Container Depots of South India by road and rail. The Port
is a congestion-free one and has the personalized service to its users. The Port also has the
distinction of zero incidence of pilferage.

record traffic of 174.29 lakh tonnes during 2009-10  as against 154.94 lakh tonnes in the previous
year registering an increase of 12.49%. Container traffic has touched an all time record of 2,89,817
TEUs which is an increase of 11.13% over the previous year’s 2,60,784 TEUs. 1270 vessels
cleared during 2009-10  as against 1085 in the previous year, showing an increase of 17.05%.
66. The Committee was further informed that 45 cruise vessels visited the Port, the previous
highest being 43 in the year 2007-08. As regards the productivity parameters, the Port registered
average ship berth day output of 10829 million tonnes as against 10599 million tonnes in the
previous year and average pre-berthing detention increased to 2.08  days from 2.14 days in the
previous year.

Chennai Port
102. Chennai Port established 125 years ago, has old infrastructure which is inadequate meet the
demands of the modern day transport sector. Normally, reserve capacity of 30% is required at each
Port to take care of the maintenance works at the berths, approaches, equipments, etc. Hence,
there is need to create additional capacity as the Port is handling volumes wel1 above its rated
capacity of 50 million tonnes. This shortfall is now being addressed by upgrading the existing
berths (modernization of Jawahar Dock and other berths in the inner harbour in stages) and also
creating new berths such as the Second Container Terminal at Dr. Ambedkar Dock, Mega Container
Terminal at North of Bharathi Dock etc.
103. Due to historical reasons, the draft at the inner harbour berths of Chennai Ports varies
between 7.91 meters and 11 meters which are not adequate to handle the larger vessels prevalent
in the international trade. There is also need to handle higher parcel sizes and modern cargoes such
as containerized cargoes and project cargoes in line with the directions of the Ministry to provide
draft of atleast 14 meters in all channels, basins and alongside berths. The NMDP scheme of
Deepening of channels, berths and basins was formulated and works are being taken up in stages.
The work has been completed in Jawahar Dock and other berths will be taken up in a phased
manner. Capital dredging will follow the berth modernization.
104. As in the case of infrastructure upgradation, there is a need to increase loading and
discharge rates of vessels at berths so that Ports are able to compete at the international level. As
part of this process, Chennai Port Trust is replacing old cranes with modern high capacity cranes
in a phased manner. In addition, a semi-mechanized closed coal conveyor system has been installed
for improving productivity levels in coal handling (from Jawahar Dock East berths to the coal plots
at the Southern end of the Port) and also reduce dust pollution levels.
105. A Multi-pronged strategy is being adopted for better utilization of the available land area
especially as Chennai Port Trust suffers physical constraints in expansion due to the Port being
surrounded by Chennai city on 3 sides. The problem is being addressed by:-
a. Dismantling old sheds/warehouses which have outlived their useful lives to create open
space.
b. Creating additional area by reclaiming land from the sea as in the case of area of 7.85

109. The Committee notes that the traffic handled by the Major Ports has increased from
313.53 million tonnes in 2002-03 to 560.96 million tonnes during 2009-10. The aggregate
capacity of the Major Ports has also increased from 362.75 million tonnes per annum to
628.03 million tonnes during that period. The Committee is, however, constrained to note
that despite the increase in capacity and traffic handled by the Major Ports, there has been
negligible growth in efficiency parameter at Major Ports. For example, average turn around
time has gone up from 4.24 tonnes in 2001-02 to 4.5 tonnes in 2009-10 and also the average
pre-berthing detention time has increased from 11.04 hours in 2000-01 to 12.19 hours in
2010-11. Though the average output per ship per berth day has gone up substantially  from
6961 tonnes in 2000-01 to 12133 tonnes in 2010-11 (up to December, 2010) which however,
is not a matter of great solace as all our Major Ports are far behind as efficient as
compared to some of the Ports in nearby countries. Even today the majority of Indian
exports/imports are carried through transshipment centers at Ports in Colombo, Singapore
and Dubai. The average dwell time at Indian Major Ports is 1.88 days for import and 3.78
days for export of containers in comparison to the dwell time at Singapore Port is 0.6 days
for import or export of containers.

equipment/machinery at the Ports were very old, installed decades ago and the right type

machinery. The Committee further recommends that Government should enhance the

DREDGING
122. Most Indian Ports operate at drafts less than 10 meters (33 ft). This directly undermines
their capability to service large international ship. Thus lower draft restricts cargo movement to a
large extent capacity. In fact, internationally the average draft is 14.5 meters but even in the biggest
container port of India, Jawaharlal Nehru Port (JNPT) average draft is 12.5 meters. Colombo Port,
for example has (18.5 meters) draft, which can easily handle new-generation ships carrying over
6,000 containers. The result is that large container ships, which are bound for India, are forced
to be routed via Ports where they can be broken down into smaller cargos, for onward
transportation. Thus transportation cost and travel time increases. Deepening projects critical for
Indian Ports for their competitiveness, has been largely neglected.
123. The Ministry informed that with the increase in size of the cargo vessels in the shipping
trade, almost all the Ports are not capable of receiving bigger vessels with the drafts available at
present. Deepening of channel and berth basins, therefore, becomes necessary. Dredging
Corporation of India (DCI) is catering to maintenance/capital dredging requirements to the extent
of 65% for maintenance dredging.
124. The Committee was also informed that most of our Major Ports are incurring expenditure
annually for both capital and maintenance dredging in order to achieve adequate draft. Some Ports
have also received gross budgetary support (GBS) from the Government for undertaking dredging
activities. In the recent past, this includes Paradip Port and currently projects funded by
Government support are being undertaken at Cochin and Tuticorin Ports as wall.

phase-I of capital dredging to provide depth of 15 meters CD at berth areas of marine liquid, coal

internal resources and commercial borrowings.

16 meters to handle container vessels. The total quantity of materials to be dredged in phase II
is of the order of 20 Million cubic meter at a total estimated cost of around Rs.440 crores to be
funded from internal resources and commercial borrowings. In addition to dredging, EPL is
required to invest about Rs.500  crores on vital road and rail connectivity projects over the next

rd and 4 th coal berth from where the upcoming

unavoidable to maintain adequate depth and width for the safe navigation of ship calling at Kandla
The dredging expenditure is getting increased year after year and an amount of Rs.120 crores is
likely to be spent during this fiscal. There are restrictions on night navigation because of long

contract is pending for final approval of the Government. The dredging to increase the draught of

obtained. The capacity addition is 2.40 million TEUs. There are some tender related litigations in
the Supreme Court and the final implementation of the project is subjected to the final verdict.

the Paradip Port has taken up two projects. The deepening of existing entrance and approach
channel has been taken up which will cost an amount of Rs.253.36 crores. The project was

enable the Port to handle 1,25,000 DWT vessels. Further the project for enhancement of draught
at existing Dock system from 12.5 meters to 14.0 meters to cater Panamax Vessels is proposed
at the cost of Rs.40 crores.
140. The dredging plays an important role in facing the challenges of increased vessel
sizes and handling operations of the Port. With the development in the Port sector the
requirement of dredging has also increased manifolds. Nowadays, modern vessels like
panamax and supermax cargo ships are used by the international carriers, these vessels
require draft of 14 meters or more. However, Committee is constrained to note that
execution of dredging projects has not been given due priority and as a result thereof the
capacity addition programme of the Major Ports have affected substantially. The Committee
notes that a number of projects have been taken up for capital dredging of the berths. The
Ennore Port have plans to carry out capital dredging for berth area of iron ore to 18
meters, port basin to l8.5 meters, channel to 20 meters to handle cape size  bulk carriers.
Under phase II of the capital dredging programme the Ennore Port is likely to incur an
amount of Rs.440 crores from internal resources and commercial borrowings. They have
also planned to carry out phase III of dredging to provide a depth of 18 meters to TNEB’s

26
third and fourth coal berths, which are likely to cost an amount of Rs.200 crores. Kandla
Port is also facing problem of lack of adequate natural depth in approach channel from the
open sea. The dredging expenditure there has increased year after year and an amount of
Rs.120 crores was likely to be spent during the year 2010-11. Committee also notes that
Tuticorin Port is having draft of about 10.7 meters only which is highly inadequate when
compared to the neighboring Indian Major Ports and international Port of Colombo. The
award of contract for deepening the approach channel and basin to cater to 12.8 meters
draught vessels is pending for final approval of the Government.
141. In the case of Mangalore Port, the Committee has been informed that there is
annual requirement of dredging of around 5 million cubic meters and the dredger is
required for almost 100 days in a year.
142. Both capital and maintenance is an important component for cargo handling capacity
and to increase the efficiency of the Indian Major Ports. The Committee recommends that
projects taken up/proposed to be taken up are executed in a time bound manner. The
Committee further recommend the projects of dredging of Tuticorin Port should be
processed seriously and promptly as project is critical for survival of a Port. The Committee
also finds that cost estimates were prepared for 5 years back in the case of New Mangalore
Port need review in view of the increase in the cost as on date. The Committee also
recommends to explore the Possibility of making available dredger exclusively for the use
in New Mangalore Port as its requirement of dredger is for almost 100 days in a year. The
Committee notes that there has been increase in expenditure on dredging by the Major
Ports. During 2000-01 around 17% of the total operating expenditure of Major Ports has
increased to around 20% in 2005-06. The Committee, therefore recommend that in view of
the increase in the expenditure on dredging, the Government of India should take the
responsibility and prepare a long term plan for financing the dredging operations in all the
Major Ports.
143. The Committee also recommends that the approach channel of all Major Ports of the
country should be treated at par with national water ways and therefore funding for the
same should be taken up by the Government of India.
144. The Committee is constrained to note that Government of India have not been able
to implement their decision of making 100% reimbursement or dredging subsidy to KoPT
which is already reeling under a severe financial crisis. The Committee notes that an
amount of Rs.873.12 crores is receivable by KoPT from the Government of India. The
Committee observes with vested interest the Government of India have imposed certain
decisions on the Ports/DCI and DCI was forced to shift its dredgers to SSCP ignoring the
critical operational requirement of dredging of KoPT. This led to dispute between KoPT and
DCI as the latter could not fulfil its commitment of dredging as per the agreement and was
imposed penalty of 20% by KoPT. This in turn affected the already deteriorating financial
health of DCI. The Committee recommends that the Government of India should take steps
to release an amount of Rs.873.12 crores to KoPT towards dredging subsidy. The committee
also recommends that amount held by KoPT as penalty on  DCI should be met by the
Government of India because it was their decision which forced DCI to remove dredger
from Haldia to SSCP.

th

constrained to note that the company has been given shabby treatment and forced to carry
out certain commercial activities totally against the financial canons, It appears that there

interests in the Government to make DCI a sick unit which resulted in taking over of the

Rail Connectivity
161. The success of a sea port depends on the availability of cheap and better connectivity to
the mainland. The importance of rail lines comes in this point of view. Evacuation of cargo by rail,
plays an important role in the shipping sector as transport by rail constitute the major portion of
cargo handling by Ports. To facilitate the Ports, Indian Railway has provided its network upto the
port. Besides this, the Railways and Ports are in partnership for funding the projects.
Mumbai Port
162. The Mumbai Port owns and operates its own Railway which is connected to the broad
gauge main lines of Central and Western Railways at its interchange Railway Yard at Wadala. The
railway runs for about 10 km. of straight route between Ballard pier and Wadala and has an
extensive network of track of about 100 km. For improvement of Rail connectivity a dedicated
goods line between Wadala and Kurla is proposed with a cost of Rs.131 crore. This 4.4 km. long
goods line will establish a direct link between Mumbai Port Railway networks to the Central
Railway network and will remove the existing constraint of limited and erratic availability of
window for movement of goods trains in and out of Port via harbour line. The project is scheduled
to be completed in March, 2012. The Committee was informed that to handle future volumes,
Mumbai Port would require 18 cargo loading-tracks by 2025-26, out of which 3 are already
available-hence requiring 15 additional ones.

30
163. Further, creation of additional RCD for containers, identify land estates with Mumbai Port
for laying new lines and direct haulage of Central/Western Railway locomotive to within the Docks
are also required.
Jawaharlal Nehru Port
164. The Jawaharlal Nehru Port is well connected to the main hinterland with a double railway
line up to Panvel. The rail infrastructure at the port is saturated and there are no extra tines and
stabling yards for accommodating large number of container trains transporting the cargo. A rail
yard near the Port would cater to the EXIM cargo traffic of all the terminals.
165. The Ministry of Railway has initiated a mammoth project of a Dedicated Freight Corridor
from JN Port to New Delhi to evacuate the cargo being handled at JN Port. The project is likely
to be taken up within 1-2 years. As a part of this project, the doubling of existing lines, up to
the Port’s ICD terminals is under the active consideration of Dedicated Freight Corridor
Corporation India Ltd.

yard at Panambur under the Southern Railway but located inside the port area has four captive lines

The Committee fails to understand the rationale behind imposing the additional charges on
certain trade. The Ministry of Shipping may take up the matter with the Ministry of
Railways to do away the practice of  levying of additional charges by the Konkan Railways.
The Committee also finds that development of  rail link from coastal to hinter-land is faced
with environmental hindrances as the rail link needs to be developed cutting across the
western ghat section. The Committee recommends that the matter may be taken up with
the Ministry of Environment and Forest to  find out the viable solution for the issue. The
Committee finds that Paradip Port is facing the problem of  cargo evacuation due to the
absence of adequate rail link to the hinterland. The Committee also recommends that
matter may be taken up with the Ministry of Railways to ensure that the Paradip-
Haridaspur rail link project is completed within the targeted period. The Committee also
recommends exploring the possibility of connecting the Paradip with the Kolkata and
Visakhapatnam Ports by rail. The Committee is of the view that this will enhance the
business opportunities, traffic sharing and development of specific cargo facilities at these
three Major Ports. The Committee also notes that there is inadequate supply of rakes by
the Ministry of Railways which has affected the evacuation of  containers/cargo from the
port premises. The Committee also finds that cargo carrying capacity by road and rail, is
below the requirement which has affected quick movement of  cargo.
187. The Committee recommends that high capacity rail loading equipment and efficient
traffic regulation may be arranged for better cargo movement from the Port. The
Committee also recommends that Railways should bring ‘dedicated trains’ rather than
‘mixed trains’ which only add to increase of work load due to inter-terminal trucking.
Environment friendly stack yards and warehouses for the projected future traffic movement
should be established. The efficiency of  the present day rail service may be made in
accordance with the developing needs of  the services and shortage of engines while loading,
may be met with in order to minimize the waiting periods of the wagons.
188. Cochin Port situated in Willingdon Island is not well connected. However, even after
completion of the full electrification of  rail lines in Kerala, the stretch of railway from
Ernakulam Junction to  Willington Island has not been electrified due to objection from

34
Indian Navy. Railway is constructing a new bridge across Vembanad Lake connecting
Ernakulam to Willington Island. However, the effective utitisation of this facility and the
rail connectivity to the Port can be made only though electrification of  this stretch of
railway. The Committee would like to seek clarification as to why NoC was not obtained
from Ministry of  Defence before taking up the work of electrification of rail line. The
Committee recommends that the matter should be sorted out with Naval authorities and
Ministry of  Defence.

No. 11 to 16 at Kandla, the road up to 12
th cargo berth has been completed and road network up

major state roads in the D.K. District.

36

Paradip Port
201. The port of Paradip is basically a service provider to the traders and suppliers and the main
economic activities of the Port is earning of foreign exchange through export/import of cargoes like
Coal, Iron Ore, Charge chrome, Ferro Chrome, Chrome Ore and other ores, fertilizer and sugar
etc. A Good transport network is a vital requirement for steady supply of Cargoes in accordance
with the demand of the trader. NH-5A connects Paradip to various important roads the country.
The roads from Cuttack to Paradip has vital role in the ever growth of Paradip Port.
202. The Committee has observed that road congestion is a regular feature at the NH-5A because
of over crowding of trucks on both the ways. 1t was learnt that over 3000 loaded trucks are
coming and going to the Paradip Port on a daily basis. The Committee was informed that the sorry
state of the NH-5A started since the super cyclone in the year 1999. However, the little bit of
efforts made for the road development is lagging behind of schedule and about 50% of thus 90
km. road is still under various stages of construction causing difficulties to the general public, huge
losses of resources such as fuel, time and even causes very dear to innocent lives of people at
the time of emergency medical assistance. However, the information provided by the NHAI states
that only the rehabilitation of old Mahanadi bridge at 67
th km. is only pending. The Committee
noticed that the work of NH 5A was started on February 2004 with a total estimated cost of
Rs.327.77 crores. The project was to be completed after 3 years. However, the works are yet to
be over even a lapse of nearly 7 years.

NHAI to execute the projects of road connectivity and 12 km. road connecting the Port to National
Highway has been commissioned. Improvement of 2-lane roads to 4-lane roads and construction
of flyovers/ramps etc. will be taken-up in co-ordination with NHAI.

37
Cochin Port
204. The hinterland connection of the Cochin Port is through the Ernakulam city. The Wellingdon
Island, where Cochin Port is situated was then connected to the mainland of Ernakulam though a
bridge. The city has now developed many folds and traffic from the Port has also increased
tremendously. This will further increase in future. Though one more bridge connecting, Wellingdon
Island to the Cochin bye-pass has been constructed, evacuation of cargo through the heavily
congested city areas is causing severe 1ocal and social problems. As such possibility of providing

over the NH by-pass at several places, the container traffic as well as the city traffic has been
posing a serious problem in the city areas. Since the ICTT Vallarpadam proposed to handle 2.5
million TEUs per year, the movement of container trucks will excessively increase. The
Committee recommends that in order to ease the road congestion, National Waterway
passing through hinterland of Cochin Port may be developed.
Kolkata Port
205. Kolkata Port is well connected with National and State highways, railways and national
waterways, KDS is connected with NH-6, NH-2 and NH-34 through city roads. NH-41 connects
HDC with NH-6 and rest of the country.
Tuticorin Port
206. The proposed dedicated freight corridor linking Tuticorin-Erode-Nagpur for the easy
movement of cargo from the central parts of the country to the port may be expedited. The
Committee hopes that the projects of 4-laning of NH 7A (47.2 km.) to Tirunelveli and NH 45B
(128.5 km.) to Madurai which are the major road connectivity to the Port will be completed as
per their scheduled completion date. The Committee also recommends that construction of
Turicorin-Kollam Express way may be materialized for the ease of road connectivity to the
Port.
Chennai Port
207. The Committee was informed that the Port is a partner in the SPV – Chennai Ennore Port
Road Company Ltd. along with NHAI, Government of Tamil Nadu and Ennore Port Ltd. for
upgrading the Northern corridor from the Port to the National Highway system. The project
estimated to cost Rs.600 crores for improving the connecting roads viz. Fishing Harbour Road
from the northern gate, Ennore expressway, Manali Oil Refinery road, TPP Road and northern

208. In order to upgrade the access to the Southern/Western corridor from the Port to the
National Highway, an elevated port link road to Maduravoyal for a length of 19 km. has been
